newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space shuttle heads for Florida landing.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space shuttle heads for Florida landing.

text.p: U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger, aboard the space shuttle Atlantis, was homeward bound on Soturday after four months in space.

Atlantis began an hour-long plunge through the atmosphere at 8:25 a.m. EDT (1225 GMT) as it orbited west of Australia. The shuttle was due to touch down at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre at 9:28 a.m. EDT (1328 GMT).
The shuttle's return to Earth was delayed 90 minutes because of low clouds over the runway.
Linenger, the fourth NASA astronaut to live and work aboard Mir, was to ride home in a cushioned reclining seat on the shuttle's lower deck.
His four-month stay on Mir was marred by a serious fire, life support problems and a near collision with an unmanned cargo craft.
The 42-year-old medical doctor and navy captain said he was determined to walk off the shuttle after its landing, despite NASA's preference for him to be carried off.
During his stay on Mir, Linenger, who lists marathon running and ocean swimming among his hobbies, was to run daily for two hours on a treadmill to keep up his strength.
Although that exercise programme was disrupted by the problems aboard Mir, NASA did not expect any complications after Linenger's return to Earth.
Long-duration space flights, away from the pull of gravity, cause bones to weaken and muscles to waste away.

If the shuttle lands as planned, Linenger will have spent 132 days in space, the second-longest mission for an American astronaut. Shannon Lucid set the current U.S. record with a 188-day stay on Mir last year.
Linenger said it would be "pure elation" to be reunited with his 18-month-old son, John, and his wife, Kathryn, who is expecting their second child in June.
